entry.title: When VFX and Practical Sets Work Together, Sometimes You Invent New Cameras
entry.summary: Whalefall" production designer Ramsey Avery tells IndieWire about the collaboration that led the filmmaking team inside the belly of a whale.
entry.content:
The first person swallowed by the rogue sperm whale in “Whalefall” wasn’t grieving diver Jay Gardiner (Austin Abrams), searching the waters off the coast of Northern California for the remains of his recently deceased father, Mitt (Josh Brolin). It was production designer Ramsey Avery, who was responsible for building a series of sets that couldn’t be easier to write into Final Draft, and couldn’t be harder to realize in real life.

INT. Whale.

Ramsey had worked with director Brian Duffield and director of photography Aaron Morton on a previous project, “No Will Save You,” and some of the folks at WETA on “The Rings of Power” series. But they all knew it would take a huge team effort and a combination of practical and digital effects in order to create the interior of the sperm whale that takes Jay on a ride both literal and spiritual. Avery and the “Whalefall” team would eventually craft five different stomach sets (some of which crossed the Pacific Ocean to get from Weta Workshops in New Zealand to the shooting tanks in Los Angeles) plus a mouth, an esophagus, and a puppet of a giant squid.

Related Stories
Ken Russell’s ‘The Devils’ Extends Theatrical Run Following Strong Box Office Debut
Watch ‘Man on the Run’ Director Morgan Neville Unpack Paul McCartney’s Life After Beatlemania

“You don’t get challenges like this. And so it just was a tremendous thing. I mean, pretty much everybody came at it with a sense of, ‘Oh, this is gonna kill us, but we’re gonna have fun while we’re doing it anyway,’” Avery told IndieWire. “I was really worried because here I am [in the research process] clicking through images of the insides of grotesque stomachs and being like, ‘They’re never gonna make this movie.’”

But no amount of tripe samples, anatomical explorations of the corpses of beached whales, nor  orthoscopic images of people sticking cameras down the throats of orcas and dolphins and horses and cows could scare off the “Whalefall” team, which conducted four different camera tests to scale up and calibrate the sets they’d need.

“In the long run, you want the emotions [of the story] to come through. So the stomach has to become a character. It’s not just about the mechanics of it but how you make things activate. The WETA team, in particular a guy by the name of Ben Milson, was really instrumental in terms of figuring out what motion you need to convey different emotions inside the whale,” Avery said. “At the same time, it was practice. Try this. Try that.”

The team practiced over four different camera tests, scaling up the stomach sets (made of silicone, latex, and also a fair bit of upholstery) each time and adding more variability in how each could be used. Each set was rigged to move differently, from a large gimbal that could achieve the big swings of the whale rising or diving, to a washing machine-type rig designed to spin, to a rig calibrated to create very specific, fine, and almost emotional movements in close-up.

Some of the stomach sets were able to be struck from the outside to create additional tension or even act against Abram’s distress, whether big spasms caused by the full weight of a grip throwing themselves against it or smaller shivers caused by tools jury-rigged out of plywood and pool noodles. “Each step of the way, we learned something and figured out something a little bit more, and came to a way that this is how we can get the camera in. And by the way, sometimes there’s two cameras. There’s two cameras, a boom, and an actor.”

It’s a feat to get all of that in. But the two cameras, boom, as well as all the LED strings used to light the stomach interior can’t stay there. The practical challenge of creating a realistic shooting environment for this truly wild and singular experience is one thing. What Avery and the VFX team realized, though, is that they’d need to digitize not just each environment, but every moment.

“Normally what we do when we build a set, and they have to scan it for visual effects [is] we’ll film out the scene, and then they’ll come in, and they’ll just scan the whole set, and that’s that. But that didn’t work because the set kept changing. The set’s always moving,” Avery said.

Enter production VFX supervisor Guillaume Rocheron, who was part of the early camera tests in order to figure out how to take the guts of what Avery was designing and render it in a digital environment. “ We had like a four or five-week period where we were kind of all on other jobs and working part-time trying to figure this out,” Avery said.

What Rocheron figured out was an infrared binocular camera that could attach to the other cameras that allowed him to capture a moving 3D scan of the set that matched every single shot. “He invented the camera, he wrote the code, and figured out a way to capture that constant motion. So we had both the actor with the right light on his face interacting actually realistically, physically, entirely with a moving set that was always the right size and shape, and the right color, and the right finishes,” Avery said.

Rocheron could translate all of that information into WETA’s digital pipeline, and enhance what had been shot, not just by painting out lights or a boom mic, but by creating that extra slimy, organic, alive quality of living tissue. Rocheron and his team painted some samples of the sets with “ either ginger ale or seltzer water, I don’t remember which, and lit it in black light, and that gave him bioluminescent drips. Then he could use that as the texturing to get the bioluminescence kind of falling off the walls,” Avery said.

There are some shots that are really just the stomach sets Avery built, but the overall effect and the emotional stress of being inside the whale is achieved through a fantastic melding of the practical and the digital, always retaining the tactile qualities of the former while adding scope and a kind of seamlessness with the latter. That’s the kind of collaboration that makes effects work, and it came about because, according to Avery, it wasn’t whales but people all the way down.

“I was the first guinea pig and the WETA guys were all in there, too, figuring out the action and pushing and pulling [the stomach] and all that stuff,” Avery said. “We all worked together as a team. It was a truly collaborative effort, and we just worked well together — and that was across two continents, you know. That was great.”

“Whalefall” is now playing in theaters.

entry.title: Ken Russell’s ‘The Devils’ Extends Theatrical Run Following Strong Box Office Debut
entry.summary: The restored version of Ken Russell's 'The Devils' will extend its theatrical engagements beyond its planned one-week run.
entry.content:
The re-release of Ken Russell‘s controversial epic “The Devils” was initially only supposed to be in theaters for one week. However, Warner Bros. Clockwork, which oversaw the restoration, announced that it will extend its run due to “popular demand.”

The film opened last weekend in 350 locations across North America. It grossed over $1.7 million for a per-screen average of $4,925. That’s a respectable result for a re-release.

Clockwork will continue to monitor ticket sales and will keep it in theaters for as long as it keeps performing, according to an individual with knowledge of its release plans. It will be in 315 locations in its second weekend.

Related Stories
Watch ‘Man on the Run’ Director Morgan Neville Unpack Paul McCartney’s Life After Beatlemania
‘Possible Love’ Review: Two Married Couples Begin to Covet Each Others’ Lives in the Latest Stunner from ‘Burning’ Director Lee Chang-dong

The NC-17 film marks the first time that an uncensored director’s cut is available to audiences everywhere. Clockwork premiered the remastered, unabridged version at Cannes and then rolled the film out at key film festivals such as Il Cinema Ritrovato, Toronto International Film Festival, New York Film Festival, Beyond Fest, BFI London Film Festival, Sitges Film Festival, and Festival Lumière.

“The Devils” stars Vanessa Redgrave and Oliver Reed. Its scabrous look at religion, power, and corruption was considered too hot to handle in 1971 (nuns simulating sexual acts with a massive cross had its detractors). Those pesky censors necessitated certain alterations upon release.

But over the decades, the film’s renown has grown and “The Devils” has been championed by movie lovers, such as Guillermo del Toro. The cut was originally reconstructed in 2004 under the supervision of Russell and the film’s editor Michael Bradsell with the collaboration of Mark Kermode and Paul Joyce. The 4K restoration was completed using the original camera negative at WB Water Tower Color, with audio restoration completed using original composite 35mm mag film at WB Sound.

An international theatrical release will follow. BFI will release the film in the U.K/ and Ireland beginning October 30. Theatrical runs will also extend to Poland (October 23), France (October 28), Australia/New Zealand (October 29), Germany/Austria (October 29), Greece (November 12), the Netherlands (November 12), and other territories.

entry.title: Watch ‘Man on the Run’ Director Morgan Neville Unpack Paul McCartney’s Life After Beatlemania
entry.summary: Neville joined IndieWire editor-in-chief Brent Lang to discuss making the definitive doc about McCarney's Wings era.
entry.content:
Morgan Neville has made documentaries about some of the most influential cultural figures in recent history, from Brian Wilson and Keith Richards to Fred Rogers and Lorne Michaels. But there’s no challenge quite like a Beatle.

His latest film, “Man on the Run,” focuses on Paul McCartney‘s decade following the end of The Beatles. The documentary captures his move to rural Scotland, the formation of his second major band Wings, and the recording of seminal albums like “McCartney” and “Ram.” It captures McCartney’s solo career with the same gravitas as Peter Jackson’s “Get Back,” shining light on an era of music that is often dismissed when compared to his earlier masterpieces.

Related Stories
‘Possible Love’ Review: Two Married Couples Begin to Covet Each Others’ Lives in the Latest Stunner from ‘Burning’ Director Lee Chang-dong
‘Clayface’ Review: A Gross Miscalculation (Emphasis on the Gross)

At IndieWire’s Art of the Doc event on Monday, October 19, Neville sat down with IndieWire editor-in-chief Brent Lang to discuss bringing the Beatle’s story to the big screen. He explained that, despite there being so many recent documentaries about The Beatles, McCartney’s Wings era offered an untold story that could shine new light on one of the greatest songwriters of all time.

“I got a call, I met with him, and I told him this film ends the day The Beatles broke up and it ends the day John Lennon dies,” Neville said of the project’s origins.

The director went on to explain that the McCartney we see for much of the film was scarred by the aftermath of his early fame and the acrimonious breakup of his band. His retreat to pastoral family life was a necessary step in reconnecting with his own musical talents.

“There was some PTSD that all of them had from going through being a Beatle. They just didn’t ever have to grow up … in certain ways they never had to deal with reality,” he said. “People were angry, and that trauma turned into anger, like ‘Why can’t you guys just get back together?’ and blaming everybody. Linda’s idea was to go off to this tiny farmhouse to the middle of nowhere in Scotland. Which sounded a little insane, but probably was the sanest decision they ever made.”

Watch the complete conversation with Neville in the video above.

National Geographic Documentary Films, part of a joint venture between The Walt Disney Company and the National Geographic Society, is committed to bringing the world premium, feature documentaries that cover timely, provocative and globally relevant stories from the very best documentary filmmakers. Its award-winning and critically acclaimed films reach 300 million people worldwide in 180 countries and 33 languages across the global National Geographic channels and direct-to-consumer platforms Disney+ and Hulu. Recent films include the Emmy-nominated winner of the IDA Award for Best Feature “The Tale of Silyan;” Oscar® and Peabody nominee “Sugarcane;” Oscar-nominated and Peabody Award winner “Bobi Wine: The People’s President;” Emmy Award winner “Lost In The Jungle;” Oscar- and BAFTA-nominated “Fire of Love;” Emmy and Peabody Award winner “The Territory;” BAFTA nominees “The Rescue” and “Becoming Cousteau;” and Oscar- and BAFTA winner “Free Solo.” For more information visit films.nationalgeographic.com, or find us on Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, and YouTube.

entry.title: ‘Possible Love’ Review: Two Married Couples Begin to Covet Each Others’ Lives in the Latest Stunner from ‘Burning’ Director Lee Chang-dong
entry.summary: Jeon Do-yeon leads a sprawling Netflix drama about the relationship between a rich documentary filmmaker and her blue-collar subjects.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 6, 2026 at the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Netflix will release “Possible Love” in theaters on Friday, October 23 before it streams beginning on November 6.]

Another heart-stopping and novelistically layered stunner from modern cinema’s most literary auteur (a fiction author himself), Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love” might be dedicated to the memory of Krzysztof Kieślowski’s “Dekalog 10,” but let’s dispel any notion of it being a remake. Conceived independently, and then lumped during pre-production into the same tribute omnibus that kicked off with Asghar Farhadi’s dreadful “Parallel Tales” at Cannes this year this film shares nothing in common with the final episode of Kieślowski’s series beyond the biblical commandment that Lee splays on screen at the very start: “Thou shalt not covet.” 

Related Stories
Japanese Cult Blockbuster ‘Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story’ to Get First U.S. Theatrical Release in December

And even then, the evidence of that instruction proves elusive in this sprawling drama about two very different couples who are brought together by the violent suppression of a workers’ strike at a major Korean metals factory. Who is coveting what, exactly? 

It’s simple enough to understand what the film’s characters want on the surface — or at least that’s true of its women. A casually rich dilettante whose pale skin glows with the same lustrousness as her salon-perfect bob, first-time director Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong, similarly cast as the rich mom in “Parasite”) hopes to make a documentary about the declining state of labor across South Korea, with a particular focus on the recent unrest at a business called SP Heavy Industries. Although we see Ye-ji pitching the project to a grant board of some kind, the presumption is that most of her funding — and all of her creative freedom — has been provided by her imperiously chiseled husband Sang-woo (Lee newcomer Zo In-sung), a trust fund type who appears to enjoy a rather frictionless existence.

On the other side of the economic divide, the plucky but sad-eyed Mi-ok (played by “Secret Sunshine” actress Jeon Do-yeon, who delivers another once-a-century performance less than 20 years since her first collaboration with Lee) is clearly willing to do whatever it takes to bring her husband back to life. One of the “dead” who lost his job and sense of purpose in the mass layoffs at SP two years ago, her taciturn and implosive Ho-seok (“Peppermint Candy” star Sul Kyung-gu) has been a shell of himself since being injured amid the crackdown that ended the ensuing strike, and Mi-ok hopes that participating in Ye-ji’s doc might allow him to process his trauma — to stop shuffling around like a zombie and snap back into the man she once fell in love with as a teenage seamstress who didn’t have any better options. That he might become a more present father to their young son Cheol, whose current rudderlessness is best expressed by his abject incompetence at Taekwondo. 

Beyond that simple baseline, the matrix of desire at work in Lee and Oh Jung-mi’s remarkably nuanced script is too slippery to pin down until the movie’s velvet gutpunch of a final scene. Yes, Mi-ok lusts after Ye-ji’s elegant wardrobe and designer handbags, and there’s an unspoken sexual charge in the air whenever she’s alone with Sang-woo (a charge that eventually sets fire to an unforgettable pre-dawn sequence on a private beach in the third act). But it would be unwisely reductive to conclude that the working-class woman is jealous of her hyper-affluent new bestie, just as it would be unhelpfully rash to assume that envy plays a more pivotal role in this story than resentment, or that a film as mottled and probing as “Possible Love” might be content to retrench the divide between Korea’s haves and have-nots. 

Lee is perfectly happy to inflame our anger towards the one percent, and the movie’s jagged script — first inspired by a similar incident at a massive Korean company more than 10 years ago — is at its broadest when poking fun at how blithely Ye-ji inserts herself into Mi-ok and Ho-seok’s blue-collar world. She wants to be a fly on the wall in their downtrodden factory town, but the pampered documentarian stands out like a Maybach at a monastery; despite growing up without a silver spoon in her mouth, she rages at her inability to code-switch back to a lower rung on the financial ladder. 

As the story goes on and Ye-ji convinces Mi-ok and Ho-seok to join them for a weekend at Sang-woo’s luxurious vacation house along the country’s western coast (all the better to entrap the couple on her turf where she can film them at all hours of the day), Lee finds a devious variety of ways to weaponize the running visual gag in which an intimate scene pans over to find Ye-ji hiding in the corner with her camera. It’s admirable that she wants to highlight how workers are being left behind as the ownership class automates their businesses in order to hoard their wealth, but Ye-ji fails to recognize the many condescending ways that she infringes upon her subjects’ dignity, as if — in a world where labor is increasingly rendered invisible from the people who profit from it — people like Mi-ok and Ho-seok should feel lucky to be seen at all. 

In contrast to Lee’s monumental and more explosive “Burning,” the story he tells here builds on an instance of terrible violence rather than building to it, but his latest film simmers to a boil at a similar clip, and likewise alternates long dialogue scenes with indelible moments of visual acuity. While it’s hard for this comparatively restrained domestic saga to compete with Jeon Jong-seo’s sunset dance along the DMZ, Lee retains his gift for whipping spectacle out of thin air — for infusing something as routine as a car ride home or a quick dip in the ocean with an overwhelming degree of silent pathos. Every moment in “Possible Love” crackles like a wicked symphony of striated socioeconomic abrasion; every gesture, comment, and detail sharpens the strange geometry that brings these people closer together at the same time as it deepens the divides that will ultimately keep them apart. 

Sometimes, in a handful of judiciously deployed moments, that geometry is expressed in skin-crawling fashion. Case in point: Sang-woo keeps an antique whistle on the living room mantle of his summer palace, and the resident “house fairy” — a seemingly non-verbal groundskeeper who Sang-woo used to play with when they were kids — is conditioned to come running whenever he blows on it. For the most part, however, the distance between the film’s characters is conveyed in subtler terms; in the confidence of Sang-woo’s upright posture, the brittleness of Mi-ok’s wavy hair, and the brusque impenetrability of Ho-seok’s blank stare, which doesn’t suggest the absence of an inner life so much as it betrays the constant struggle to bottle up his demons. He’s a prisoner of the pain that Ye-ji breezily documents like a tourist. 

The careful attention that Lee pays to his characters’ bodies and how they wear them pays off — enormously — after “Possible Love” relocates to Sang-woo’s summer home for this 164-minute film’s last hour (“This is like a house from a novel I haven’t read,” Mi-ok gawps over dinner). Between a night of drunken karaoke and a few pre-dawn strolls along the mansion’s private beach, the movie’s financially driven exploration of freedom and power begin to assume a more physical dimension, a transition which threatens to confuse the dynamics that have otherwise tethered everyone to their roles; this is where Jeon seizes control, her raw and marbled performance reaching a state of self-preservation so primal that it renders the rest of the characters senseless. 

“Possible Love” takes brilliant — if unnerving — pleasure in leveling the playing field between its two couples, but those shifty indulgences are too freighted with reality to feel like wish fulfillment. The film isn’t naive enough to pretend that its “poor” characters might ever achieve true equilibrium with its rich ones, nor is it patronizing enough to suggest that there’s some kind of implicit dignity to being exploited by the carelessness of late capitalism. Ho-seok is not a holy sufferer, he’s a profoundly broken and embittered man whose plight speaks to the hopelessness of fighting back against a system that’s designed to trample people like him, and Lee is far more interested in rendering his pain than he is in “solving” it. 

The ultimate power of “Possible Love,” which grows in the mind after it’s over (and greatly rewards any repeat viewings), is rooted in neither wanton despair nor false optimism. Despite being steeped in the sadness and frustration of the working class, Lee’s drama uses its film-within-a-film construct to refract the moral valences of labor through the prism of what people actually earn through their work. 

Slumming it as a documentarian as she builds towards her dream of being a narrative filmmaker (“Imagining things is my hobby” is maybe not what you want to hear from the person directing a documentary about your life), Ye-ji is a victim of her own second-hand affluence — the seamlessness of her life has life has made it so that she has to performatively “method act” in order to get close to her subjects and shoot anything real. Her observational technique is a parody of the invisible labor that she laments noticing the first time during a trip to a luxurious Qattari hotel, but she can’t even see people like Mi-ok and Ho-seok unless she contrives a scenario for them to exist for her camera. 

For his part, Sang-woo’s work is so frictionless that he can buy and sell entire companies from his laptop while sipping a latte, and his marriage to Ye-ji feels like it’s laminated in plastic. They passively snipe at each other in short bursts so as not to get any dirt on the bedsheets, and relegate all of their latent desires to the blind spots that rich people create so that they don’t have to see the world beyond their own wealth. 

By contrast, Mi-ok and Ho-seok have no choice but to confront the hardships that have been visited upon them, and to want for things so badly they can never lose sight of the work they’ve put into each other. Their lives are principled upon a possible love, because they don’t have the luxury of pretending there’s any other kind. Yes, their history together — fleshed out in a series of perfectly modulated flashbacks — is clumsy and imperfect, and their financial prospects for the future are tenuous at best, but they will never have to covet what this world still offers to people for free. Mi-ok and Ho-seok have always felt as if the moon shined only for them at night, and the final moments of this gently shattering and astonishingly well-shaded drama exalt in the freedom they give to each other by saving its glow for themselves. 

Grade: A

“Possible Love” premiered at the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Netflix will release it in theaters on Friday, October 23, and on Netflix on Friday, November 6.

entry.title: ‘Clayface’ Review: A Gross Miscalculation (Emphasis on the Gross)
entry.summary: James Watkins' gory, goopy R-rated body horror is an offbeat addition to the DCU's increasingly erratic output.
entry.content:
Three films into its latest “chapter” (this one subtitled “Gods and Monsters”), James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DCU can’t be faulted for making interesting choices. Hell, at least they’re making choices at all. Kicking off their incarnation of the latest run of comic book movies with “Superman” was unquestionably smart (it’s Superman! you know him!), even if its follow-up “Supergirl” was destined to divide audiences (even if this critic quite liked it, surely there are other reasons why some members of this seemingly dedicated audience didn’t, no matter its quality).

Enter: “Clayface.” Another set of execs and filmmakers wouldn’t have bellied up to this grim, gross anti-hero to round out their first trio of movies meant to reset a massive franchise. But does that kind of ambition and vision pay off in James Watkins‘ goopy, gory, decidedly R-rated body horror feature? Not so much, even as open-minded audiences will likely admire the big swings on offer here. It’s certainly different, and for comic book movie fans absolutely bored to death by the same old stuff, it’s something of a respite. Yet, divorced from all that, Watkins’ film confounds much more than it compels.

Related Stories
Japanese Cult Blockbuster ‘Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story’ to Get First U.S. Theatrical Release in December
Watch Ava Duvernay Explain Why the 14th Amendment Is So Much More Than Birthright Citizenship

A working knowledge of Clayface lore is not required to understand the film — the script from Mike Flangan and Hossein Amini lays out the essentials with ease, before collapsing in the film’s second half — though it’s perhaps helpful to know that that he’s always been imagined as a Batman adversary. Fair enough. Those bones of the story (bones! those will soon be in short supply!) hint at perhaps why he was chosen for this early story in the new DCU: get some Batman winks in there, introduce us to Gotham City, toy with some dark underbelly stuff.

Flanagan and Amini also latch on to another bit of early Clayface backstory: he’s an actor, a pretty natty way to make horrific facial scarring really hurt. Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries, very good at conveying genuine pathos under gobs of makeup and VFX) is a Gotham City native, a wrong-side-of-the-tracks kid who is on the cusp of superstardom. When we first meet him, he’s about to be nominated for a major award (on-screen graphics don’t say what it is, though someone later calls it an Academy Award, sure), fielding great new offers, and trying to stay grounded. His best pal Corey (Joshua James) helps, as do his frequent mentions of his fraught early life.

Matt is, by all accounts, a nice guy. He introduces himself to the pretty flight attendant on the private jet! He’s sweet to his agent! He goes back home to Gotham to chat with other rising young performers! But Matt is also — and this is something the film can never quite square — a bit too easily swayed by a pretty face and a night out at the club. When an alluring young lady (Joana Ribeiro) makes eyes at him across the dance floor, he can’t resist (even when she tells him she’s an aspiring actor; run, dude!). Thank goodness Corey is on hand to remind Matt that his new paramour is the girlfriend of local mob boss Markos Szabo (David Dencik). Too bad that Matt just doesn’t care.

Well, that’s life in Gotham City (perpetually damp, grimy, and graffiti-covered), and when Matt and Mia wake up the next morning, they’re surrounded by Markos and his band of (lightly Dick Tracy-coded) toughs. Markos, understandably ticked off (and somehow aware that Corey had told Matt that Mia was taken), takes out all his toxic masculine rage on Matt’s gorgeous face, carving him up and leaving him to deal with it. Gross, goopy, gory, bloody, and just plain meaty, Matt’s physical ailments aren’t shied away from at all, and Watkins’ dedication to going full body horror is admirable.

And the attendant facial disfigurations are bad enough (remember, Matt is an actor, he really needs his face), but what follows is arguably worse. Believing he might find justice (in Gotham City?!), Matt tries to take legal action against Markos. What follows: character assassinations, horrific surgeries, financial lootings, and the total decimation of life as he knows it. Which is all to say, when Matt meets Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), he’s willing to do anything to get a slice of his life back. And Caitlyn sure loves slicing, dicing, and toying with “nanocells” (not clay, sorry) that Matt believes can fix his visage.

Great news! It does! Well, for a time. Hellbent on getting his life back (via his face), Matt overdoses on those damn nanocells and promptly becomes a monster, both figuratively and literally. Gone is our sweet young actor, instead replaced by a snarling, revenge-obsessed freak who is scared (and then delighted) to discover he can shift his face into whatever he wants, whoever he wants, whenever he wants. (A subplot about how Caitlyn can calm him feels terribly shoehorned in to add an icky romance dimension.)

Increasingly muddy effects and plotting don’t do Matt’s transformations many favors — the film does much better, clever work when he’s just slipping between different faces, zipping behind a door and emerging as someone else. The mechanics of those transformations aren’t clear either: are they subconscious? does he need to think of someone to “become” them? touch them? can he make their clothes too? or is that also skin? We’re spinning out just thinking on it. At least these moments allow some supporting stars, including Eddie Marsan and James, the chance to have quite a bit of fun playing Matt “playing” their characters.

A few meaty set pieces help, too, including a truly stomach-churning sequence set on an airplane (turbulence and nanocells are a bad mix) and a third act revenge-driven visit to the club that gives Rhys Harries plenty to chew on (to say nothing of some of Matt’s biggest foes). But the uneven nature of the film, its plotting, its character motivations, and its aims only become bigger and bloodier as the film winds on. Malleable, sure, but this ambitious misfire can never conform to one shape, one final form, or one good idea.

Grade: C+

Warner Bros. will release “Clayface” in theaters on Friday, October 23.

entry.title: Tom Cruise to Be Honored with AFI Life Achievement Award
entry.summary: Tom Cruise has been named as the recipient of the 52nd Life Achievement Award from the American Film Institute.
entry.content:
Tom Cruise will be the 52nd recipient of the American Film Institute‘s prestigious life achievement award. The “Mission: Impossible” and “Digger” star will be feted with a gala tribute at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles on April 24.

“Tom Cruise is a global icon,” said AFI board of trustees chair Kathleen Kennedy wrote in a statement. “As an actor and producer, he brings an extraordinary commitment to everything he does. What I especially admire is his deep belief in movies and their ability to bring people together. That passion has made him an extraordinary ambassador for American film around the world. It is AFI’s honor to present him with the 52nd AFI Life Achievement Award.”

Related Stories
Why Seeing ‘Digger’ in VistaVision Could Change Your Mind About the Tom Cruise Box Office Flop
After the ‘Digger’ Disaster, What Should Tom Cruise Do Next?

Now 64 years old, Cruise has remained one of the industry’s most prominent stars since he launched in the 1980’s with leading roles in “Risky Business,” “Top Gun,” and “The Color of Money.” As the unshakably determined secret agent Ethan Hunt, he led the “Mission: Impossible” action series across 30 years, starring in eight entries and subjecting himself to increasingly daredevil stunt-work as they went along. Other blockbuster titles have included “Rain Man,” “A Few Good Men,” “Collateral,” “Edge of Tomorrow,” and “Interview with the Vampire.”

Cruise has also been nominated for three Oscars: in lead actor for 1989’s “Born on the Fourth of July” and 1996’s “Jerry Maguire,” and in supporting actor for 1999’s “Magnolia.” He was also an Academy Award nominee as a producer for 2022’s “Top Gun: Maverick,” which was nominated for best picture. In 2025, he received an honorary Oscar from the Academy at the organization’s annual Governor’s Awards.

The star also finds himself back in the awards conversation this year for his lead turn in Alejandro González Iñárritu’s “Digger.” Cruise will next be seen in the sequel “Days of Thunder 2.”

The Life Achievement Award is AFI’s highest honor recognizing a career in the film industry. John Ford was the first recipient in 1973, with other notable names including Orson Welles, Alfred Hitchcock, James Stewart, Steven Spielberg, Martin Scorsese, Jack Lemmon, Tom Hanks, Robert De Niro, Meryl Streep, Jane Fonda, and Diane Keaton. More recent honorees include Julia Andrews, Nicole Kidman, and Francis Ford Coppola.

This year’s ceremony honored Eddie Murphy, with a recording of the tribute later premiering on Netflix. The event included Bill Burr, Dave Chappelle, Arsenio Hall, Spike Lee, Mike Myers, Chris Rock, and Stevie Wonder among its presenters and performers.

entry.title: Neon Boards ‘NAZA’ to Expand Distribution for Documentary About Israel’s Military Strikes on Gaza
entry.summary: Neon will release "NAZA," a documentary about Israel's military strikes on Gaza from the "No Other Land" directors — self-distributed until now.
entry.content:
Neon has joined the release of “NAZA,” a documentary composed of anonymous interviews with 24 members of the Israeli military that details the country’s airstrikes on Gaza and the killing of Palestinian civilians.

The partnership marks a major sea change within the distribution market. Filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor‘s last documentary “No Other Land” (co-directed with Hamdan Ballal and Basel Adra), about Israeli settler violence in Palestine’s occupied West Bank, went without a U.S. distribution partner in 2024 — a development that, at the time, Abraham said he “read it as something that’s completely political.” Many in the industry have speculated that traditional distributors had concluded that documentaries about Israel and Palestine were too controversial to do business with in the U.S. Despite being released independently, “No Other Land” ended up grossing $3.6 million in theaters worldwide and won the Oscar for best documentary feature.

Related Stories
Audiences Want to See Documentaries About Gaza, Israel, and Palestine — Why Are Distributors Still Scared?
Box Office: ‘NAZA,’ Documentary About Israel’s Attacks on Gaza That Was Too Hot for Distributors, Crosses $500,000

For the “NAZA” release partnership, Neon will “work with the filmmakers to expand its footprint and to reach larger audiences and communities.” More exact details on how the distributor will support the film are yet to be disclosed.

After premiering at Venice Film Festival, where it was embraced by critics and won the special jury prize, “NAZA” immediately set an independent theatrical release in the U.S. and abroad. After opening in the U.S. on September 30, the film passed a $500,000 gross less than two weeks into its plan to play 85 theaters across 30 cities. The newspaper The Guardian, which produced “NAZA,” is planning to make the feature available to stream its website for free in November.

“Yuval and Rachel have created one of the best films of the year; it’s an extraordinary work of art and eyewitness testimony that stands alongside landmark documentaries like Laura Poitras’ ‘Citizenfour’ and Joshua Oppenheimer’s ‘The Act of Killing,'” reads a statement from Neon. “At the heart of Neon’s mission is a commitment to championing the best cinema from around the world. We’re proud to join the incredible team already working on the film and help bring it to the widest audience possible.”

Prior to the Neon deal, “NAZA” had already secured distribution plans across 50 countries. The film is produced by The Guardian with James Wilson’s JW Films banner, in association with Placeholder Films and Unseen Hand. “The Zone of Interest” director Jonathan Glazer is an executive producer. MK2 Films negotiated the deal with Neon.

entry.title: Japanese Cult Blockbuster ‘Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story’ to Get First U.S. Theatrical Release in December
entry.summary: "Rex: A Dinosaur Story" was one of the most expensive films ever made in Japan, but its release was cut short when its director was arrested.
entry.content:
Kani Releasing will bring the 1993 feature “Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story” stateside in December, setting its first-ever U.S. theatrical release. The Christmas-set comedy, which features animatronics by Italian effects guru and “E.T. the Extra Terrestrial” design creator Carlo Rambaldi, will receive a one-week run at New York’s independent theater Metrograph on December 11, with openings in Chicago, Seattle, Austin, and other markets to follow.

Released in Japan on July 3, 1993, “Rex” was heavily marketed and positioned to contend with the ranks of rival U.S. tentpoles. The blockbuster ambitions are best illustrated by the production’s recruitment of Rambaldi. The effects artist began his career in the Italian film industry, working filmmakers like Dario Argento and Mario Bava, before making a jump to Hollywood and contributing to productions like “Close Encounters of the Third Kind,” “Alien,” and “Dune.” “Rex” was certainly chasing the child-actor and animatronic two-hander dramatics of “E.T.,” which were made possible by Rambaldi’s work designing the character.

Related Stories
Watch Ava Duvernay Explain Why the 14th Amendment Is So Much More Than Birthright Citizenship
Gen Z Feels ‘Doomed’ Watching AI, but Gen Alpha Feels Differently

“Rex” was actually a strong box office draw in Japan, grossing 2.2 billion yen in its theatrical run to rank as the seventh-highest-grossing release of 1993. But at a production budget of 2 billion yen, the family film was still a money loser in theaters.

As Kani Releasing describes it, original distributor Shochiku also pulled “Rex” from theaters after the film’s then-dominant director Haruki Kadokawa was accused of instructing an aide to smuggle cocaine from the United States. Though the blockbuster director argued his innocence, he was convicted in 1994 and served a two-and-a-half year sentence. (Shortly after, he had managed to direct another feature: the 1997 adaptation of Yasutaka Tsutsui’s sci-fi novel “The Girl Who Leapt Through Time.”)

The North American release comes after Japan Society programmed a new remaster during its 2026 edition of New York’s Japan Cuts festival in July. Kani Releasing is handling distribution, adding to its catalogue of repertory titles and rising directors from Asian film industries.

“Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story” will play Metrograph to open its “Dinosauria” series. Running through January 3, other titles programmed include “Fantasia,” “Godzilla,” “Journey to the Beginning of Time,” “Jurassic Park,” “The Land Before Time,” and “The Tree of Life.”

entry.title: Watch Ava Duvernay Explain Why the 14th Amendment Is So Much More Than Birthright Citizenship
entry.summary: At IndieWire's Art of the Doc event, the '13th' director explained why her Netflix follow-up contained much more than she initially expected.
entry.content:
When Ava DuVernay approached Netflix about making a follow-up to “13th,” her acclaimed documentary about the legacy of the constitutional amendment that abolished slavery, she thought it was a fairly straightforward proposition. The 14th Amendment is best known for offering U.S. citizenship to everyone born in America, a right that is frequently attacked by the current administration.

That seemed like enough material for another film, but the two-year process of making “14th” taught her that the amendment contains so much more.

During a conversation with IndieWire’s Chris O’Falt at our Art of the Doc event in Los Angeles, DuVernay explained how the project evolved over time.

Related Stories
Gen Z Feels ‘Doomed’ Watching AI, but Gen Alpha Feels Differently
A New Australian Horror Import Imagines ‘Obsession’ from a Very Different Perspective

“I thought we were talking about birthright citizenship. That’s what I sold to Netflix,” DuVernay said with a laugh. “We worked on it for two years. The whole first year we were making a movie about birthright citizenship. And then we started seeing the other parts get attacked. The parts where I was like ‘This is too hard, I don’t want to focus on these other parts.’ But when we started to hear them coming up in those headlines, you couldn’t leave that out.”

The duo discussed how the constitutional amendment “flies under the radar” compared to more notable ones that everyone memorizes in history class, despite containing important protections like the Equal Protection Clause and the Due Process Clause.

“It does [fly under the radar],” she said. “Which is wild, because it holds in it the rights that we abide by.I didn’t realize the depth that was in the 14th amendment. One of our folks in the film says it’s a constitution in and of itself. I didn’t know that the 13th, 14th, and 15th truly created a new constitution that got clicked onto the first one.”

Ultimately, DuVernay hoped that making her documentary can help steer the conversation in a way that allows future generations to see the value of these legal protections that we were previously able to take for granted.

“It really comes to who gets to tell the story, and whose voice is the loudest,” she said. “That really becomes what history is. It’s the stories we tell each other.”

Watch the complete conversation with DuVernay in the video above.

National Geographic Documentary Films, part of a joint venture between The Walt Disney Company and the National Geographic Society, is committed to bringing the world premium, feature documentaries that cover timely, provocative and globally relevant stories from the very best documentary filmmakers. Its award-winning and critically acclaimed films reach 300 million people worldwide in 180 countries and 33 languages across the global National Geographic channels and direct-to-consumer platforms Disney+ and Hulu. Recent films include the Emmy-nominated winner of the IDA Award for Best Feature “The Tale of Silyan;” Oscar® and Peabody nominee “Sugarcane;” Oscar-nominated and Peabody Award winner “Bobi Wine: The People’s President;” Emmy Award winner “Lost In The Jungle;” Oscar- and BAFTA-nominated “Fire of Love;” Emmy and Peabody Award winner “The Territory;” BAFTA nominees “The Rescue” and “Becoming Cousteau;” and Oscar- and BAFTA winner “Free Solo.” For more information visit films.nationalgeographic.com, or find us on Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, and YouTube.

entry.title: Gen Z Feels ‘Doomed’ Watching AI, but Gen Alpha Feels Differently
entry.summary: Over 30 percent of young people feel either "doomed" or "scared" when watching AI content, but a study found notable differences in age groups.
entry.content:
One of the more inexplicably popular sources of AI slop today is “Fruit Love Island,” an AI-generated TikTok parody series in which anthropomorphized fruits with abs and cleavage flirt and mingle in 60-second ripoffs of “Love Island.” It is as mind-numbingly dumb as it sounds, and though TikTok started suppressing and demonetizing the videos due to being low quality AI, per the series’ own website blog posts, it persists and has tens of millions of views.

Suffice it to say, your teenager or pre-teen may very well have come across these videos or could easily be obsessed with them. But depending on just how old your teen is, their mileage may vary.

Related Stories
‘Sinner Supper Club,’ a Gay Mumblegore Ghost Story, Sells to Factory 25
Nathan Fielder Was Not Supposed to Be in ‘You Can See Everything’

A new study from UCLA and the Center for Scholars and Storytellers called “Rewrite This! How Gen Z and Gen Alpha are Redefining Modern Storytelling” showed that while a majority of young people actually view artificially generated content and stories positively, there is a noticeable shift in how they feel as today’s kids get older.

The study found that 53.8 percent of people between ages 10 and 24 described emotions of either “fascinated” or “excited,” while only 32.1 percent used the phrases “doomed” or “scared.” However, when asked to complete the sentence, “Watching a story with AI in it makes me feel…,” those who felt “doom” compared to “excitement” went up considerably as the survey participants aged up. 27.4 percent of 18-24 year olds used the emotion “doom” compared to just 9.7 percent of those aged 10-13 and 25.1 percent of those 14-18 years old. Nearly half of those between 10-13 felt “excitement” when watching AI content.

The study notes that many of the respondents’ feelings about AI come from AI-native videos they find on their social media feeds. “Fruit Love Island” was one such example, but turns out there are plenty of other examples of AI fruit littering TikTok. It also mentions brainrot memes like “tung tung tung sahur” (no clue) and AI soap operas via vertical, microdramas from ReelShort, DramaBox, Drama Wave, and Pocket Films.

This all feels significant because the narrative tends to be that Hollywood and tech companies are pushing AI even though a lot of people simply hate it and are even repulsed when they see endless amounts of slop on their feeds or in any sort of film or TV. But while the study doesn’t draw any grand conclusions, it suggests there might be a generation gap between Gen Z and the emerging Generation Alpha, who might feel differently and look more favorably at AI than other young people.

“I’d like to see AI portrayed in a balanced and realistic way, showing both its benefits and potential risks,” one 13-year-old polled for the study said. “It would be interesting to see AI helping people solve problems, learn new things, and improve everyday life while also exploring questions about trust, privacy, creativity, and human control.” Smart kid.

This is the fifth year of the study from UCLA and the Center for Scholars and Storytellers. Last year we covered the study with the takeaway that while many young people still love movies and series, many of them are not watching on TVs or in theaters themselves and instead are viewing through YouTube, on phones and laptops, or unconventionally on social media.

This year’s study touched on some of the same questions and found that more than half of young people still ranked “see a movie at the movie theater” as the top weekend activity with their friends if geography and money were not a constraint. But it also had some other new areas of study including what themes they most prefer to see depicted on screen (hopeful messages over partying and drinking), whether they want to see social media influencers in their movies and shows (surprisingly, no), and even if the movies did a good job depicting neurodivergence on screen (only 22.7 percent said “yes, most of the time”).

Find more from the study here.

entry.title: A New Australian Horror Import Imagines ‘Obsession’ from a Very Different Perspective
entry.summary: Film critic, author, and horror expert Alexandra Heller-Nicholas writes about taking her teenage son to see “The Only One."
entry.content:
Alexandra Heller-Nicholas is a multi-award-winning Australian film critic and the author of eleven books on cult, horror, and exploitation cinema, including the book “1000 Women in Horror,” which was adapted to a feature documentary for Shudder in 2026. In 2024, she appeared in Alexandre O. Philippe’s “Texas Chain Saw Massacre” legacy documentary “Chain Reactions” alongside Stephen King, Patton Oswalt, Karyn Kusama, and Takashi Miike, which won the Venice Classics Award for Best Documentary on Cinema at the Venice Film Festival.

“It’s like if ‘Obsession’ was from the perspective of the woman actually being obsessed over.”

Related Stories
‘Sinner Supper Club,’ a Gay Mumblegore Ghost Story, Sells to Factory 25
Nathan Fielder Was Not Supposed to Be in ‘You Can See Everything’

I have just left an advance screening of Michael Schwarz’s new horror film “The Only One” with my teenage son, and the conversation is taking a surprising turn than what I perhaps expected. “Why is it the woman’s problem if men are weird about them? Why is it her job to help them figure it out?”

I’ve written a bunch of books of cult, horror, and exploitation film criticism, including monographs on rape-revenge cinema (yikes!) and “1000 Women in Horror,” my 2020 book which was adapted into a documentary for the horror streaming service Shudder in 2025, directed by Canadian filmmaker Donna Davies. I love going to horror movies with my kid because I get to experience them through different eyes to my own. But I am always a little self-conscious that our post-movie discourse leaves me sounding a little preachy, a little didactic, and, well, a little… parental.

But this kid clearly does not need spoon-feeding and is fully equipped to figure things out by himself. Unlike most of the horror movies we see together, this screening is unusual because I am here largely in a civilian capacity. We weren’t here for the rigorous social analysis of contemporary horror, but rather for largely personal reasons: one of my oldest friends, Martyn Pedler, co-wrote the film with Marek Polgar.

Martyn and I moved to the south-eastern Australian city of Melbourne over thirty years ago from the nation’s tiny and exceedingly dull capital, Canberra. Gender politics aside, “The Only One” most immediately spoke to me of that palpable anxiety from being an adult returning home to the small town you outgrew. It’s “Welcome Home Roxy Carmichael” with a body count.

“The Only One” begins in Los Angeles, where Zoe (Mel Jarnson) is working as a barista to pay the rent when her dreams of superstardom remain acutely unfulfilled. Begrudgingly returning home to the small town she left with big dreams and a string of broken hearts trailing behind her, with the help of her best friend and the town’s token goth (Saphira Moran) — there’s always one — the two women face the growing realization that someone is killing off Zoe’s many exes, one by one. Dressed as a classically cartoonish Prince Charming no less, the killer slash-and-dices his way through a list of everyone Zoe dated at high school. In doing so, an array of future possible victims return to Zoe’s life – some for better, and some for worse.

Based on this brief synopsis alone, that some of these exes (most notably the truly repugnant local cop, played by Ben O’Toole) default to slut-shaming Zoe is as depressing as it is seemingly inevitable. Refreshingly, however, the film is unambiguous: this is creepy and wrong, a reflection of his flawed character, not hers.

While “The Only One” was in production long before Curry Barker’s “Obsession” was even released, it thus provides a flip side to the same conversation about gender, agency, and that age-old question: “Why are so many men just so damned weird about women who aren’t interested in them?”

While “The Only One” might have inadvertently stumbled into the same discursive terrain as one of the biggest surprise horror hits of recent years, its heritage can be traced back much earlier. From romance-themed horror films like George Mihalka’s “My Bloody Valentine” (1981) and the long-tail of gothic romantic literature from Bram Stoker’s “Dracula” (1897) to Stephanie Meyer’s “Twilight” novels, this century alone has seen a boom of horror-romances in the indie film space especially, with Justin Benson and Aaron Moorhead’s “Spring” (2014) and Jeremy Gardner and Christian Stella’s “After Midnight” (2019) surely at the top of the list.

When it comes to Australian horror, we punch well above our weight on this front. In 2025, Australian filmmaker Michael Shanks had a commercial and critical hit on his hands with the wholly singular body horror film “Together” with Dave Franco and Alison Brie. And sixteen years earlier, national horror hero Sean Byrne won hearts and minds at genre fests around the world with his deliciously twisted heartsick-aspiring-prom-queen-run-amok cult classic, “The Loved Ones.”

But “The Only One” continues the legacy of one film in particular. While the boom period of late ‘90s/early ‘00s teen slashers are linked most immediately to multiplex blockbusters like the “Scream” and “I Know What You Did Last Summer” franchises, in an admittedly uncharacteristic display of patriotism my favorite deep cuts were made by Australian filmmakers: Geoffrey Wright’s “Cherry Falls” (1999) and Jamie Blanks’ “Urban Legend” (1998).

If “The Only One” has one true ancestor, however, it is Blanks’ latter slasher film “Valentine” (2001) with “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” star David Boreanaz. Both films are drenched with perverse subversions of romantic iconography to gleefully playful effect, right down to their respective Cupid and Prince Charming killer masks which look like they could have been crafted by the same person.

And while “The Only One” pulls no punches when it comes to being wholly Team Zoe as she contends with a steady stream of creepy, obsessive guys, the famously ambiguous ending of Blanks’ “Valentine” refuses to grant us with the neat happily ever after we initially think we might be getting.

“Valentine” and “The Only One” were made by different filmmakers at different times, but with Blanks’ unexpected death in March this year at only 54 years old, Schwarz’s film feels like an accidental homage to one of the best horror filmmakers this country has ever produced.

That younger audiences can readily identify how “The Only One” taps into the same ideas as “Obsession” underscores how the film is much more than the retro pastiche its early ’00s horror vibes might at first suggest. But at the same time, “The Only One” is very much a film that continues a successful tradition of Australian romance-themed horror, wearing its heart on its sleeve for the genre classics that came before it.

“The Only One” world premiered at MONSTER Fest and will have its international premiere at the 2026 SOHO Horror Film Festival in the UK next month.

entry.title: ‘Sinner Supper Club,’ a Gay Mumblegore Ghost Story, Sells to Factory 25
entry.summary: 'Sinner Supper Club,' a gay mumblegore ghost story shot on an iPhone, has sold to Factory 25.
entry.content:
Factory 25, a Brooklyn-based independent film distribution company, has acquired worldwide rights to Daisy Rosato and Nora Kaye’s first feature film “Sinner Supper Club” at the New York premiere of the film at NewFest. The film is described as a “gay mumblegore ghost story” about friends reuniting to throw a “wake” for Genevieve, who has been priced out of New York City. As the night progresses and a heatwave traps them together, their long-ignored problems boil over….and then their dead friend shows up.

The film was shot in six days on an iPhone through improvisation. It is an homage to the scrappy and experimental filmmaking that characterized both the mumblegore and Dogme 95 movements. As part of production, the filmmakers wrote a manifesto, one that explored what it means to make a film in the 2020’s, with characters that represent the queer and transgender and gender nonconforming community.

Related Stories
Nathan Fielder Was Not Supposed to Be in ‘You Can See Everything’
$1 Million Box Office Haul for ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’ Provides a Release Template for the Smallest of Indies

The cast includes Elise Kibler, Ashil Lee, Genevieve Simon, Jayae Riley Jr., Sophie Sagan-Gutherz, Kaye and Rosato. In addition to directing and appearing in the film, Kaye and Rosato wrote the screenplay. Rosato also served as the cinematographer.

Factory 25 is planning a spring 2027 theatrical release followed by a digital and Blu-ray release. Factory 25 has released such films as “Funny Ha Ha,” “Ham on Rye,” “Happer’s Comet,” “Actual People,” “This Closeness,” “Family Portrait,” and “Queens of the Qing Dynasty.”

NewFest was founded in 1988 in response to the AIDS crisis. The New York LGBTQ+ Film Festival has been a tentpole of NYC’s queer cultural scene. In the subsequent years, NewFest has expanded into a film and media organization with year-long programs to serve all facets of the LGBTQ+ community.
